_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: He slaughtered it and its daughter’s daughter: [so far] he has committed no transgression.
rashi:a1.2: And afterward slaughtered its daughter: [the daughter] of the first. Now it turns out that he slaughtered [her] with two prohibitions: [with] the first [animal], “it and its offspring,” [the first being the mother and] the third [its offspring]; and [with] the second, “its offspring and it,” for its offspring is the second and “it” is the third. Therefore he incurs eighty [lashes] according to Sumakhos, even though they are one name.
rashi:a4.1: Differentiated bodies: for it is because of the first and the second [animals] that these two prohibitions came upon the third. But here the bodies are not differentiated.
rashi:a5.1: Perhaps like Rabbi Abbahu: but here, even though it is through her daughter, her daughter’s daughter and her son’s daughter that the elder woman became forbidden to him by three prohibitions, there are no differentiated bodies in her.
rashi:a5.2: One lewdness: that he is liable only one [offering] for a woman, her daughter, her daughter’s daughter and her son’s daughter in one act of intercourse, as in our mishna; and these are his mother-in-law, his mother-in-law’s mother and his father-in-law’s mother.
rashi:a6.2: Emmaus: the name of the town.
rashi:a6.3: One who engages in intercourse with his sister, etc.: it is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a8.1: Gemara. Aren’t they differentiated names: for three distinct prohibitions apply to them.
rashi:a11.1: One name: [the prohibition] for a menstruating woman, “you shall not approach.”
rashi:a11.2: Who is his father’s sister: as explained below, with “a wicked man, the son of a wicked man.”
rashi:a13.1: He has uncovered his sister’s nakedness: it is explained in the first chapter (above, Keritot 2b) that this [phrase] is left over for him for this exposition.
rashi:a15.1: He engaged in intercourse with her: with one of all the forbidden women, and again engaged in intercourse with her, during one lapse of awareness.
rashi:a16.1: With five menstruating women: during one lapse of awareness.
rashi:a16.2: Since he caused them: each one to bring a sin offering, that is, five sin offerings; therefore he too brings five sin offerings. But [for] five acts of intercourse with one forbidden woman during one lapse of awareness, she too brings only one, and so does he.
rashi:a17.1: He during one lapse of awareness: whether he [had] five acts of intercourse with five forbidden women, or five acts of intercourse with each one.
rashi:a17.2: And they during five lapses of awareness [Rashi’s text reads “they,” plural, where the printed Gemara reads “she”]: each of them became aware between one act of intercourse and the next. He is liable only one for each one, and each of them is liable five, that is, for every act of intercourse. Evidently, even though he caused each of them to bring five sin offerings, he need not bring more than one for each. Some books read: “he during one lapse of awareness and she during five lapses of awareness,” and [then] it speaks of a single forbidden woman. It is a euphemistic expression. (The printed text ends with an abbreviation, ויש״ר כח״ו, left untranslated.)
rashi:a19.1: He reaped: a fig-bulk on Shabbat, which is the measure, and again reaped during one lapse of awareness. What would Rabbi Eliezer say to me?
rashi:a21.1: Two acts of intercourse cannot be combined: therefore they count [as separate]. [But] reaping two fig-bulks can be combined and reaped at the same time.
rashi:a23.1: Rabbi Eliezer deems one liable for subcategories of labor in a situation of primary categories of labor: that if he performed a primary category and a subcategory during one lapse of awareness, he is liable two. Hence [for] primary and primary, for example where he reaped and reaped, where each is a primary category of labor, he is exempt from one.
rashi:a25.1: What are we dealing with here: in what Rabbi Eliezer taught, etc., from which we inferred that [for] primary and primary he is exempt.
rashi:a26.1: A dalit: it is a [climbing] vine (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a26.2: Trellised over a fig tree: and there were figs on the fig tree and no grapes on the vine, and he needed to cut the vine for firewood, and he cut the fruit of the fig tree and the branch of the vine at the same time. He is liable two: one for the fruit of the fig tree, which is reaping, and one for the vine branch, which is a subcategory of reaping, as we hold (Shabbat 73b) that one who prunes and needs the wood [performs] a subcategory of reaping. Therefore he is liable two even though [he did it] at the same time, since the names are differentiated, this a primary category and that a subcategory, and the bodies are differentiated, as they are two trees.
rashi:a27.1: Correspondingly, with regard to reaped and reaped: from which we inferred that [for] primary and primary he is exempt, for example where he reaped two fig-bulks at the same time; for then he did not do two [acts], and he did them at the same time, and there are no differentiated bodies or names either. But [if] he reaped and reaped again, where he performed two labors during one lapse of awareness, Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable.
rashi:a28.1: Mishna. A dangling limb in an animal: mostly torn off and attached by a little.
rashi:a28.2: What is it: does it impart impurity as a limb from a living creature, as though it had been torn off completely? For we hold in [the chapter] HaOr VeHaRotev (Ḥullin 128b) that a limb from a living creature imparts impurity like a carcass.
rashi:a28.3: A limb: torn off a person completely imparts impurity like a corpse, in [the chapter] HaOr VeHaRotev (Ḥullin 129b); and a dangling one, which is still attached a little, is pure.
tosafot:a4.1: Sumakhos says this only with regard to a mother and its offspring, where the bodies are differentiated: and with regard to a wife’s sister too, if he was married to two women and engaged in intercourse with a third who is the sister of both of them, of this one on the mother’s side and of that one on the father’s side, Sumakhos deems him liable for both.
tosafot:a6.1: Who went to purchase an animal for the feast, etc.: [this is told] to make known their praise, that even though they were busy, they were occupied with words of Torah.
tosafot:a8.1: Aren’t they differentiated names: and even though above, with regard to forbidden relations, the verse “a woman” is needed to make him liable for each woman even though the bodies are differentiated, nevertheless it was obvious to Rabbi Akiva that where the bodies are differentiated he is liable for each one.
tosafot:a12.1: This can be refuted: what about five wives, etc.: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua, who made the a fortiori inference, hold that the matter depends only on the names.
tosafot:a13.1: He has uncovered his sister’s nakedness: Rabbeinu Barukh asked: why does [the Gemara] not cite the karet that is written with regard to his sister, which the Rabbis need for this, and instead cites that of Rabbi Yitzḥak? One can say that it cites the one that is plainer. We find the like in Sanhedrin (34b) and in Megilla (20a).
tosafot:a13.2: To render him liable for his sister, etc.: one should not ask how [the Gemara] knows to set it in such a case, where all three are one sister; say that it speaks of entirely separate women, such as his daughter’s daughter and his daughter-in-law. [One should not ask this,] for the verse speaks of sisterhood. But it is difficult: [as for the rules of] a comprehensive or an added prohibition, how does he know that here it is a prohibition [that takes effect] all at once?
tosafot:a28.1: A dangling limb in a person is pure: in [the chapter] HaOr VeHaRotev [the Gemara] derives [the law of] an animal from creeping animals. It is puzzling: from where do we know that [the dangling limb of] a person is pure?
gershom:a1.1: [Printed note: up to here belongs to 14b.] Sumakhos says: he incurs eighty: one because of “it and its daughter” and one because of “its daughter and it,” for what difference is it to me whether it is “it and its daughter” or “its daughter and it”; so he is liable two. And the first tanna, who says forty, holds that they are one name.
gershom:a2.1: Because the bodies are differentiated: for he slaughtered three animals and violated two prohibitions. But [in the case of] one who engages in intercourse with his mother-in-law, where the bodies are not differentiated, he holds like Rabbi Abbahu, that he is liable only one; [Rabbi Abbahu] said: “a woman and her daughter… her son’s daughter and her daughter’s daughter… they are near kinswomen; it is lewdness”: the verse rendered them all one lewdness, since all of them bear the name of his wife’s daughter. All the more so with his mother-in-law, which is one name and one body.
gershom:a3.1: What is it: is he liable one for all of them? Because it is one name of sister.
gershom:a4.1: Or is he liable for each and every one? Since they are differentiated bodies.
gershom:a5.1: They said to him: we did not hear, but, etc. And we see that the matters are a fortiori: it is explained in the Gemara.
gershom:a6.1: If we say it is as it teaches: [one who engages in intercourse] with his sister, with his father’s sister and with his mother’s sister, why does he ask whether he is liable one for all of them? They are differentiated names and differentiated bodies.
gershom:a7.1: Rather, they could answer him from “his sister” at the end of [the verse] “a man who takes his sister,” which is superfluous: to make him liable for his sister who is his father’s sister and who is his mother’s sister, making him liable for each name.
gershom:a9.1: He engaged in intercourse with her: with one of all the forbidden women, and again engaged in intercourse with her. And since he caused them to be liable an offering for each one, he too is liable an offering for each one.
gershom:a10.1: But isn’t it taught: he during one lapse of awareness: that he engaged in intercourse with one of the forbidden women five times during one lapse of awareness, and she during five lapses of awareness, for she became aware between each one; he is liable only one offering and she is liable for each one. Evidently, even though he caused her five offerings by engaging in intercourse with her five times, he is liable only one.
gershom:a11.1: Rather, say: it is for this reason that they concede in [the case of] his five menstruating wives: since the bodies are differentiated.
gershom:a12.1: He reaped a fig-bulk: on Shabbat, and again reaped a fig-bulk.
gershom:a13.1: What is the reason of Rabbi Eliezer there, with one who engaged in intercourse with her and again engaged in intercourse with her? Because he performed two prohibitions, since it is impossible to combine two acts of intercourse into one. But with reaping, since he can reap two fig-bulks at the same time, say that he is liable only one.
gershom:a14.1: Rabbi Eliezer deems one liable for subcategories of labor in a situation of primary categories of labor: when he performed the subcategories together with the primaries, he is liable for the subcategories too, since it resembles the primary and is not exactly like the primary. And this is what we say in Bava Kamma, “according to Rabbi Eliezer, who deems one liable for a subcategory in a situation of a primary”: it is this. Hence [for] primary and primary, for example where he reaped and again reaped, he is exempt and is liable only one.
gershom:a15.1: What are we dealing with here: in which subcategory in a situation of a primary does he deem one liable? A climbing vine trellised over a fig tree, where he cut the cluster and the fig at the same time; that is why he is liable, for they are two kinds: harvesting grapes is the primary, and gathering the fig is the subcategory. And why is harvesting grapes a primary category of labor, when it is not written in the count of primary labors? Since harvesting grapes and reaping are written in one verse, “That which grows of itself of your harvest you shall not reap, and the grapes of your undressed vine you shall not gather,” evidently both are primary categories of labor.
gershom:a16.1: Correspondingly, with regard to reaped and reaped, where he is exempt, as was inferred: [for] primary and primary at the same time he is exempt, for example where he reaped a fig-bulk at the same time. But [if] he reaped and reaped again [and again] reaped, he is liable [for each one]; that is, [where he did it] in the usual way.
gershom:a17.1: A dangling limb in an animal: part of which has separated from it; [the question is] whether those who eat of it become impure as with a limb torn from a living creature, or not. They said to him: we did not hear, but we heard, etc.
gershom:a18.1: [Printed note: up to here belongs to 15a.] And so would those afflicted with boils: he did not mean those literally afflicted with boils, but [anyone with] any wound on account of which a limb dangles.
gershom:b1.1: [Each] would go on Passover eve to the doctor, and the doctor would cut that dangling limb until he left a hairbreadth of it attached to the body, and he would impale that dangling limb, fixing it in the ground with the dangling limb [on it]; and the owner of the limb would pull away from it, the hair[breadth] would be torn, and the limb would remain there. And that [man], the owner of the limb, would perform his Paschal offering in purity, since the dangling limb had already been cut off from him. And even before it was cut off he was pure to perform the Paschal offering, as it says that a dangling limb in a person is pure; but it teaches us something more: that even when he cut it and severed it in this way, the doctor and the owner of the limb are pure, for the limb did not render him impure at the moment it separated from him. For we establish in the Gemara that it is [a case] where they are removed with all their force: he tore that hair[breadth] away forcefully and quickly, so that it did not linger at all to render him impure.
gershom:b2.1: And we see that the matters are a fortiori: the Gemara explains what the a fortiori is.
gershom:b3.1: Just as a person, who imparts impurity while alive: [as] a zav and one impure from a corpse.
gershom:b4.1: One who wipes the leek: grass; for example, a leek that was full of rainwater, and he wipes off with his finger the rain on the leek so that it will fall from it. And likewise one who squeezes the rainwater in his hair and in his garment so that it will come out.
gershom:b5.1: The liquids within it: that is, as long as the water is on them, the water does not count as liquid to render [food] susceptible if impurity touches it, and it is not under “if [water] be put.”
gershom:b6.1: What is released from it: from the leek, or from the hair or from the garment. Once they have come out, they count as liquids that render [food] susceptible, and they are under “if [water] be put.”
gershom:b7.1: And the leek itself: which impurity touched while the water was on it. Even though it was not rendered susceptible at the time of contact, it was rendered susceptible at the time the water separated from it, for we said that what is released from it is under “if [water] be put.”
gershom:b8.1: But we learned: he would go, etc.
gershom:b9.1: Even though they squeezed their garments, and there is so much water in them that the water flows down from the upper side of the garment to the lower side of the garment, even so the water is pure and did not become impure because of the zav and the one impure from a corpse, for it does not count as liquid, either to render susceptible or to receive impurity, until it has emerged from all of it, from the entire garment.
gershom:b10.1: Once they have emerged from all of it, they render susceptible. And this water is pure, for the garments did not render it impure, since it counts as liquid only after it has emerged.
gershom:b11.1: And Rav Yosef said: why is the water pure? Let it become impure because of the garments at the moment of separation! Because at the moment they separated from them, they spurted from them with all their force and did not remain in the garments at all, so [the garments] did not render them impure.
gershom:b12.1: And we see that the matters are a fortiori: it is explained in the Gemara: just as one offering, where the bodies are not differentiated, etc.
gershom:b13.1: Rabbi Akiva said to him: if it is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai that he is liable for each one, we will accept it.
gershom:b14.1: And if for inference: that is, but if it is not a halakha and you wish to infer it a fortiori, there is a response to that inference, that it is not so.
gershom:b15.1: If you said with regard to misuse: it is logical that he should be liable for each one there, since [the Torah] was stringent with misuse, making one who feeds like one who eats and one who gives benefit like one who derives benefit. This is as is said in [tractate] Me’ila: [when] the agent carried out his agency, the householder is liable for misuse, even though the householder neither ate it nor benefited, he is liable for misuse just as his agent, who ate and benefited.
gershom:b16.1: He joined misuse over an extended period: [if] he ate consecrated food worth one peruta, even across ten days, it combines to a peruta and he is liable for misuse.
gershom:b17.1: Would you say with regard to notar, which has none of these: for one is liable for notar only for an olive-bulk [eaten] within the time it takes to eat a half-loaf. Therefore it is not logical that he should be liable for each one, as with misuse.
gershom:b18.1: What is difficult for Rabbi Shimon, that he said: not so did he ask them?
gershom:b19.1: This is what is difficult for him: he [Rabbi Yehoshua] seeks to derive one who slaughters outside from one who eats, who is liable for misuse for each one. And it is difficult for him: what about one who eats? It is logical that he is liable for each one, since he derives benefit; but one who slaughters does not derive benefit.
gershom:b20.1: Rather, he asked them about one who eats notar from five offerings, etc.
gershom:b21.1: And for not being known about them: that is, if he is uncertain whether he ate five pieces of notar in five pots during five lapses of awareness, he must bring a sin offering for each one, since by all opinions awarenesses divide; and so too [if he is uncertain whether he ate, he brings] a provisional guilt offering for each one.
gershom:b22.1: From five offerings: even during one lapse of awareness he brings a sin offering for each one, and for not being known, etc.
gershom:b23.1: The principle of the matter, etc. But if he ate, etc.: this [clause], if he ate five pieces from one offering in five pots before the sprinkling of the blood, he is liable for each one due to misuse, is [stated] by all opinions. And it says “before the sprinkling of the blood” because after the sprinkling there is no misuse, for it has already had a time of permission for the priests.
rashi:b1.1: Those afflicted with boils: their limbs fall off.
rashi:b1.2: And he would cut it: not for the sake of purity, since before this too he is pure, but so that he not be repulsive at the festival with the dangling limb.
rashi:b1.3: Until he would leave it like a hair: and he does not cut it off completely, so that the one who cuts it not become impure, for he touches it at the moment of separation.
rashi:b1.4: And impale it: the limb, on a thorn attached to the ground or to the wall; and he, the sick man, would pull away, and the limb would be torn off by itself.
rashi:b2.1: A fortiori: it is explained in the Gemara: [if] a person, who imparts impurity while alive, [and] who receives impurity while alive, [even so his dangling limb does not impart impurity, all the more so an animal, which does not receive impurity while alive].
rashi:b3.1: Gemara. One who wipes the leek: who crushes the leek [kaflut], which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b3.2: One who squeezes out water in his hair: for example, one who comes out of the bathhouse and dries himself with a towel.
rashi:b3.3: The liquids within it: within the leek are not under “if [water] be put,” for they are of no account, since they are absorbed.
rashi:b3.4: And those released from it are under “if [water] be put”: if they fell on seeds.
rashi:b4.1: And the leek itself: after the liquids came out of it, it was rendered susceptible, even though it did not touch them after they came out.
rashi:b5.1: (What is the reason, etc.) It should render the person impure: [the person] afflicted with boils.
rashi:b6.1: Removed with all their force: that he pulled himself away forcefully and it was torn off forcefully, and there is no contact at the moment of separation. But the leek’s water comes out gently; once it has come out it is immediately of account, and before it falls to the ground it touches [the leek] at the moment of separation.
rashi:b7.1: A zav or one impure from a corpse who were walking along the road and rain fell: on their garments. Even though the zav himself squeezed them, [running his hand] down his garment so that the water would fall, those liquids that run down the garment from top to bottom are pure and do not render impure a person who touches them, for they are of no account, since they are destined to be absorbed in the lower hem of the garment.
rashi:b8.1: Once they have emerged from all of it, they render susceptible: if they fell on seeds. And they are pure, for they do not render the seeds impure unless the zav touches them after they have emerged from all of it. And what is written in the latter clause, “only after they have emerged from his body,” is not part of our text.
rashi:b10.1: Mishna. He is liable: for misuse, for each pot, if he ate them before the sprinkling of the blood.
rashi:b10.2: A fortiori: it is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b13.1: If it is a halakha: that you received from your teacher that he is liable for each of the offerings, we will accept it from you.
rashi:b13.2: And if for inference: that you derive it a fortiori from misuse, there is a response.
rashi:b14.1: One who feeds is like one who eats: that if he gave consecrated food to his fellow, he is liable as though he had eaten it himself; for we hold that the one who takes consecrated property out to non-sacred use is the one who misused it, and not the one to whom it was given.
rashi:b14.2: And one who gives benefit is like one who derives benefit: with something that is not eaten.
rashi:b15.1: He joined misuse over an extended period: that if he derived benefit worth half a peruta today, and half a peruta any time from now until three years, they combine for an offering. Below, in the chapter Safek Akhal Ḥelev (Keritot 18b), it derives this from “commit a trespass [timol ma’al],” [a doubled expression that] amplifies.
rashi:b16.1: What is difficult for Rabbi Shimon: what proof is there for one who slaughters outside [the Temple] from one who eats of an offering before the sprinkling [of the blood]?
rashi:b21.1: Not known: that there were five pieces of notar and five permitted pieces before him, and it is not known which he ate, whether the five of notar or the five permitted ones.
rashi:b22.1: During five lapses of awareness: and he ate notar from one offering; he is liable five for notar, since lapses of awareness divide.
rashi:b22.2: From five offerings: [if] he ate notar during one lapse of awareness, he is liable five, since the bodies are differentiated. Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Eliezer hold in accordance with Rabbi Akiva in the mishna of Rabbi Shimon [so the printed Rashi reads; the baraita here names Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda].
rashi:b23.1: But if he ate five pieces, etc. [Rashi’s text reads “But”]: we have returned to the first tanna, who spoke in the first clause of five pieces of notar from one offering; and this is what he is saying: with regard to misuse, I concede that pots divide.
rashi:b24.1: Before the sprinkling of the blood: misuse applies; but once the blood has been sprinkled, since it has had a time of permission for the priests, there is no longer misuse. So it is explained in Menaḥot, in the chapter HaTekhelet (Menaḥot 47b).
tosafot:b3.1: One who wipes the leek: Rashi explained in his commentary: who crushes the leek [kaflut]. This is difficult: if so, these are fruit juices, and fruit juices do not render [food] susceptible. It is further difficult: it says that [the liquid] in his hair, for one who squeezes in his hair, is not under “if [water] be put,” while what comes out of it is under “if [water] be put”; and Rashi explained that he squeezed his hair after coming out of the bathhouse. If so, why is what is in his hair not under “if [water] be put”? Wasn’t it desired at the outset? And we say (Makhshirin 1:1): any liquid that was desired at the outset, even though it is not desired at the end, [renders susceptible]. Therefore the Ri explained that it speaks of rain that fell on them, and it was not desired until it came out of them.
tosafot:b3.2: One who wipes the leek: Rashi explained “crushes,” implying that he means it speaks of the juice from pressing the leek. This is not plausible, for we hold that fruit juices do not render [food] susceptible, as they are not called liquids. And the Riva explained: “wipes,” that he smoothed it with his finger or his nails to remove the rainwater on it, similar to one who squeezes his hair and his garment.
tosafot:b3.3: And those released from it, after they are released, are under “if [water] be put”: even though [water put] so that the wall not be damaged is not under “if [water] be put,” there it is because he does not want it to come. Here too, even though he did not want it at the outset, nevertheless, since he himself presses on it to get the water out of them, he has given it significance.
tosafot:b6.1: Removed with all their force: in [the chapter] HaOr VeHaRotev [the Gemara] does not answer this way when it objects that it is impurity of a concealed place. One must say that it is a dispute of amora’im in [the chapter] Behema HaMakshah, between Ulla and Ravina, and here it follows Ravina.
tosafot:b7.1: From the upper section to the lower section are pure: Rashi explained in his commentary that it is because it is destined to be absorbed in the garment. This is difficult, for in tractate Nidda, in the chapter HaIsha (62b), it says: earthenware shards that absorbed impure liquids and fell into the airspace of an oven, when the oven is heated it is impure, because the liquids come out, even though after the heating the shards will absorb them again. Rather, one should explain that it is because it is not desired as long as it is on his garments, as with the liquids in the leek.
tosafot:b11.1: One who eats notar from five offerings, etc.: this is not like one who engages in intercourse with his five wives during one lapse of awareness, who is liable for each one according to all, for those involve two warnings: he is warned about her and she about him, as below.
tosafot:b14.1: And one who gives benefit is like one who derives benefit: and the same is true that he could have said that one who derives benefit is like one who eats, which is not so with notar. But since he stated that one who feeds is like one who eats, he states that one who gives benefit is like one who derives benefit.
tosafot:b15.1: He joined misuse, etc.: here too it could have said: what is his dilemma, etc.? Since Rabbi Akiva refutes his statement, it is obvious that he accepted it.
